lede: The letters-up Mind read the generated mini-language (12,477 sentences) or three public-domain children's books from raw letters, grew its own word vectors by Hebbian co-occurrence, and was then taught names by ±1 judgements from scripted teachers. Mind seeds 0–4 (identity codes only; the corpus order is fixed), with 95% bootstrap CIs over seeds. Exploratory, not pre-registered.

findings.text: After one taught fact (fish lives in water), the Mind proposed the other lives-in facts itself and ended every seed with all 4 gold lives-in relations confirmed. First-round relation precision was 40%, against 20% for the most co-occurring (category, word) pairs. Its kind proposals were 100% right; over three judged rounds, 75% of all its proposals were confirmed.

It sorts unknown strings by kind from letter statistics alone: 95% of made-up words and 95% of real but unseen English words were judged word-like, 83% of misspellings were recognised as variants of a known word, but only 65% of random letter strings were rejected as non-words (after reading the mini-language).

The classical baselines are at ceiling on the mini-language and beat the Mind there. With one named word per category the Mind names 91% (95% CI 86–96) of held-out words (96% when it does not ask); SGNS vectors with the same single labels name 100%. Its own vectors give 1-NN 97.0% vs SGNS 99.4%, and in one-sentence fast mapping it names 51% vs 67% for additive SGNS.

Purity = share of the top-5 neighbours in the word's category (baseline candidates: corpus words read ≥2 times, minus gold function words). disclosure:
What each arm gets. All arms read the same token stream: lex/data/grammar_corpus.txt or books_corpus.txt, one sentence per line, with no cross-sentence windows for baselines. The Mind starts from the alphabet; it learns letters, word forms and its 300-dimensional context vectors by local Hebbian rules, and names only from ±1 judgements. SGNS uses dim 100, window 2, 5 negatives, 15 epochs, minibatch SGD with backprop; PPMI-SVD uses window 2 and 100 dims; both see word tokens with spaces given. In R2 and R4 the baselines get exactly the same labelled words the scripted teachers named. In R4 they are retrained on the same filtered corpus. Tuning: none in this benchmark. The Mind runs the lead's demo configuration (theta_novel 3.9, theta_margin 0.5, centering_warmup 50, and the Reader defaults); the baseline settings were fixed before any evaluation and are identical to lex/results/baselines.json. Ceiling: in the generated grammar each category has predicates no other category uses, so one sentence identifies a word's category. SGNS names 100% of held-out words, so on this corpus the Mind can at best tie on naming accuracy. Books: only 144/510 world words occur in the books, very unevenly (1 sport, 3 instruments), so the book rows are diagnostics; there the Mind's own vectors (1-NN 25.6%) are on par with SGNS (23.3%). Zero-variance rows are explained, not hidden: the letter memory (R3, R6) and the relation machinery (R5 relation rows) do not depend on the seed-dependent identity codes, so they are identical across seeds by construction (checked in code); PPMI is deterministic. R6 caveat: the Mind's letter memory was trained on spaced text, so its segmentation is not an unsupervised result. Its own branching entropy peaks at the wrong places because end-of-word is a predicted symbol; P(end-of-word) peaks work better but still below unsupervised branching entropy. Five seeds give coarse CIs.

Post-hoc addition (lead, 2026-11-23): fast-mapping by neighbour-name vote (k = 10), chosen after inspecting seeds 0–1 of R4; reported as a separate row, per-seed values in reader_per_seed/r4_vote_posthoc.json.
